title: The Gulbarga Museum Project
about: The Government Museum of Gulbarga holds 630 stone sculptures across three galleries — Chalukyan and Rashtrakutan sculpture, colonial-era artefacts, and pieces from Sannati, a UNESCO-protected Buddhist site nearby — inside a building that's stood since 1964 and draws almost no visitors; local students I later interviewed had been taken to the Gulbarga fort on school trips, but never to the museum itself. For my final-year thesis at Srishti, in partnership with Team YUVAA, the Aga Khan Trust for Culture, and the Centre for Deccan Studies, I spent weeks in Gulbarga researching how to change that — and came out with a pop-up book, a physical installation, and an app, all built around one of the museum's most striking artefact types: hero stones.

process.title: A museum nobody visited
process.text: Gulbarga's district museum has stood since 1964 and houses 630 sculptures across three galleries, but draws almost no visitors — even local students who'd been taken to the city's fort on school trips had never set foot inside it.

process.title: Weeks in the field before any design
process.text: A recce trip through Gulbarga's forts, markets, temples, and craftspeople, then a research trip interviewing archaeologists, teachers, and students and documenting all 630 sculptures gallery by gallery — before a critical-making session became the real turning point for what to actually design.

process.title: A pop-up book, an installation, and an app
process.text: "Vandu Veerana Gaathe: Legend of a Hero," a pop-up book gamifying the museum's hero stones, evolved into "Make Your Own Hero Stone" — a physical installation where visitors assemble their own hero-stone story from characters drawn from real museum sculptures — paired with an artefact-based app that guides visitors through the galleries via QR code and archives what they build.
